registrySuggestion.title: A positive Lebesgue number from a finite subcover
registrySuggestion.description: The compact interval cover admits a finite half-radius subcover; the minimum radius is positive and its ball about any x fits inside a selected original cover member.

source.visualReview: Full supplied source page inspected at 762×1262; Proposition 3 statement and full triangle-inequality proof read. This passage has no original figure.

implementation.math: Original cover members are relative Euclidean metric balls in compact X=[a,b]. Their half-radius balls strictly cover all of X; rho=min_j radius_j/2. For every x, choose a half-ball containing x. The strict margin radius_j−|x−center_j|−rho>0 implies N_X(x,rho) is contained in that original member by the triangle inequality.
implementation.reuse: Both distinct interval/cover programs use the same Style and helper; no pixel data or shapes in Substance. Numeric cover helper accepts any finite ball family; the compact teaching layout displays at most four balls.
implementation.graphics: Native optimized line/circle/rectangle/equation shapes with subdued orange strips and selected cover member emphasis.
implementation.interactive: Both build functions accept final FigureRenderOptions, with seed/interactive overrides spread last.

verification.mathematicalChecks: Exact interval sweep rejects touching open half-balls and uncovered endpoints. Both positive witnesses checked at 1,001 points including interval endpoints, strict full-ball containment margin checked, and representative z values verified. The sweep itself establishes cover for the whole real interval rather than only sampled points.
verification.visualReview: Both fully optimized native SVGs rasterized and visually inspected; selected half/full balls and uniform ball are aligned on one affine coordinate chart with clear non-overlapping labels.
verification.rootVisualReview: Passed: parent inspected both final optimized interval-cover previews.

limits: This is an original pedagogical illustration, not a reconstruction or replacement of a source figure.
A representative compact real interval illustrates the general metric-space proof; the diagram does not claim to encode arbitrary compact metric geometry.
Metric balls are clipped to X. The extent strips do not independently encode endpoint inclusion; the predicates and metric specify that they are open relative to X.
The abstract infinite refinement is represented by a genuine finite subcover, and no finite drawing purports to enumerate all its members.
